Jish was completely destroyed and not a house was left standing. The church fell, killing 130 persons, and the old walls of the town collapsed. In all 235 people were killed, and in places the ground was fissured (AM after Thomson 1837; Waghorn 1837; Robinson 1856).

In Safet, the largest of the places affected, the northern, Jewish, section of the town was almost entirely destroyed while the southern, Moslem, section suffered far less serious damage. About two thirds of the houses in Tiberias, most of them built of stone masonry, together with a large part of the walls, the bazaar, minarets, the mosque and the church of St Peter, collapsed, killing 922 people, of whom 500 were Jews, 300 Moslems and 22 Christians, and injuring 65. These figures may include casualties from 17 settlements in the environs, which were destroyed but are not named in the returns. The castle was ruined, and its towers began to lean. The baths, which had been built in 1833, were not damaged, but the yield of the hot spring and fountains increased temporarily. The town was not restored until after 1846 ([1, 6]; Thomson 1837; 1859; Shkelov 1837; Olim 1843; Montefiori 1844; F¨ urst 1847; Beldam 1851; Robinson 1856; Pfeiffer 1856; Frankl 1858; Kerhardene 1859; Jenner 1873; Layard 1887; Italiander 1979) (AM).

In the Bahsan, fire was seen coming out of the ground
In Antioch ground movements were slow and lasted intermittently for a long time.
It is said that waves flooded the coast of Lake Tiberias, but it is not clear whether this happened before, during or after the earthquake (AM after Shkelov 1837; Kerhardene 1859).

Many houses and the Church of Our Lady collapsed, but there is no evidence that the shock caused great loss of life. A part of the rampart and 70 or 90 of its outer towers were ruined. As a result of the earthquake the River Orontes (al-Asi) changed its course, and flowed into the centre of the city, which added to the damage. This was probably due to landslides triggered by the shock upstream of Antioch.
